\section{Why we estimate this equation: the HSA Phillips curve}
\label{sec:why}
Our estimating equation is the theory-motivated counterpart of the New Keynesian
Phillips curve derived by Fujiwara--Matsuyama (2026, \emph{Journal of Monetary
Economics}) under the HSA demand system. This section states their result, maps it to
what we take to data, and makes explicit how far the empirical specification departs
from the theory.

\subsection{The HSA Phillips curve}
A final-good producer aggregates a continuum of varieties through an HSA demand system
with market-share function $s(z)$, where $z=p/A$ is a firm's price normalized by the
single price aggregator $A$ (the reference price faced by firms, an inverse index of
competitive pressure). Intermediate firms set prices under a Rotemberg adjustment cost
$\chi$ and enter endogenously with a one-period time-to-build lag. Solving the firm's
problem, PPI inflation follows (their Eq.~21)
\begin{equation}
\hat\pi_t=\beta(1-\delta)\,\mathbb E_t\hat\pi_{t+1}
+\underbrace{\frac{\zeta(z)-1}{\chi}}_{\text{slope on marginal cost}}
\big(\hat W_t-\hat Z_{P,t}-\hat p_t\big)
-\underbrace{\frac{1}{\chi}\,\frac{1-\rho(z)}{\rho(z)}}_{\text{entry / cost-push}}\hat N_t,
\label{eq:fm}
\end{equation}
where $\hat N_t$ is the (log) number of firms, $\hat W_t-\hat Z_{P,t}-\hat p_t$ is the
inverse markup (the model's measure of real marginal cost), $\zeta(z)=1-s'(z)z/s(z)>1$
is the price-elasticity function (so the flexible-price markup is
$\mu=\zeta/(\zeta-1)$), and $\rho(z)$ is the pass-through rate.

\subsection{Two ways competition enters}
\paragraph{(1) The slope is a function of the firm count (structural flattening).}
The coefficient on marginal cost, $(\zeta(z)-1)/\chi$, depends on the price elasticity
$\zeta(z)$, which through $z=p/A$ and the symmetric-equilibrium condition $s(z)=1/N$ is
a function of the firm count $N$. Rising concentration---\emph{fewer firms}, higher
markups, lower pass-through $\rho(z)$---lowers this slope, so the Phillips curve
flattens \emph{structurally}. Linearizing the slope in the low-frequency level
$\bar N_t$ of the firm count gives
\begin{equation}
\kt=\kappa_0+\delta\,\bar N_t,
\end{equation}
so a \emph{positive} $\delta$ is the theory's flattening prediction: the slope moves
with the firm count and falls as concentration rises and $N$ declines.

\paragraph{(2) Endogenous entry is a cost-push term (estimation bias).} The second
term $-\tfrac{1}{\chi}\tfrac{1-\rho(z)}{\rho(z)}\hat N_t$ appears only away from CES.
It means that the cyclical component of firm entry acts as a cost-push shock through
strategic complementarity. Omitting it biases an empirical Phillips-curve estimate
(omitted-variable problem). We retain the cyclical term explicitly with its own
coefficient $\theta_t=\theta_0+\gamma\,\bar N_t$, but set it to zero in the main
model, as discussed below.

\paragraph{CES is the irrelevant case.} Under CES, $s(z)=\gamma_{\mathrm{CES}}\,z^{1-\theta}$,
so $\zeta(z)=\theta$ is constant and pass-through is $\rho(z)=1$. The entry term
vanishes and the slope is the constant $(\theta-1)/\chi$: market concentration neither
flattens the curve nor moves inflation. This is exactly our \code{ces} benchmark, and
departing from CES (the HSA models) is what can make $\delta$ and the $\hat N_t$ term
nonzero.

\subsection{From theory to the estimating equation}
Writing the activity/inverse-markup gap as $x_t$, adding a backward-looking inertia
term ($\alpha$) and a reduced-form shock $e_t$, and decomposing the observed firm
count into trend and cycle,
\begin{equation}
N^{\mathrm{obs}}_t=\bar N_t+\hat N_t+\nu_t,
\end{equation}
where $\bar N_t$ is a random-walk-with-drift trend, $\hat N_t$ is a stationary AR(2)
gap (truncated to the stationary region), and $\nu_t\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_N^2)$ is
measurement error, the HSA Phillips curve becomes the equation we estimate:
\begin{equation}
\boxed{\;\pi_t=\alpha\,\pi_{t-1}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb E_t\pi_{t+1}
+\kt\,x_t-\theta_t\,\hat N_t+e_t,\qquad
\kt=\kappa_0+\delta\,\bar N_t,\;\;\theta_t=\theta_0+\gamma\,\bar N_t.\;}
\label{eq:est}
\end{equation}
The trend $\bar N_t$ carries the structural-flattening channel (through $\delta$); the
cycle $\hat N_t$ carries the entry cost-push channel (through $\theta_t$).

\subsection{Distance from the theory}
\label{sec:distance}
We call this exercise \emph{semi-structural} rather than structural because the
specification departs from \eqref{eq:fm} in several ways. To avoid over-reading the
coefficients, we state each:
\begin{itemize}
\item the theory is about \emph{PPI} inflation, but there is no PPI expectation
series, so we pair observed PPI with a common external expectation series and the
expectation term is not a matched structural object;
\item the theoretical regressor is real marginal cost / the inverse markup, but the
main results use the unemployment gap and the HP output gap;
\item we impose no cross-coefficient restrictions from the theory and approximate
$\kt$ as a \emph{linear} function of $\bar N_t$;
\item we add backward-looking inertia ($\alpha$), which is absent from \eqref{eq:fm};
\item expected inflation is an external survey measure (Section~\ref{sec:data});
\item the main \code{hsa\_steady} sets the cyclical-entry term $\theta_t$ to zero,
i.e.\ uses only the trend channel.
\end{itemize}
The test of $\delta>0$ is therefore best read not as a structural estimate of the deep
parameters of the Fujiwara--Matsuyama mechanism, but as a \emph{reduced-form test
consistent with its sign restriction}. The mechanism implies (i) $\delta>0$ and (ii) a
monotone decline in $\kt$ along the fall in $\bar N_t$, while $\delta=0$ (with
$\theta=0$) collapses \eqref{eq:est} to the CES benchmark---exactly the
constant-vs-time-varying comparison of Section~\ref{sec:bench}. We examine both in
Sections~\ref{sec:main}--\ref{sec:bench}.

\section{Data}
\label{sec:data}
\paragraph{Sample.} Quarterly, 1982Q1--2012Q4 ($T=124$). The re-estimation comprises a
baseline of 45 cells (3 price indices $\times$ 3 activity measures $\times$ 5 models)
and the 30 weak/tight cells of the main comparison. To these we add two inverse-markup
CES/HSA-dynamic cells that directly diagnose the theoretical slope bias, for a total of
77 cells. Deleting an interior span would incorrectly treat the state transition as
consecutive quarters, so we do not estimate non-contiguous samples. Period tables from
earlier revisions are not put on the same footing as the current 77 cells and are
excluded from the conclusions.

\paragraph{Inflation.} We compare headline CPI (\code{pi\_cpi}), core CPI
(\code{pi\_cpi\_core}), and PPI (\code{pi\_ppi}). Expected inflation $\mathbb{E}\pi$ is
the same external survey series in all specifications. Because the Survey of
Professional Forecasters does not publish a PPI forecast, the PPI specifications use
the same expectation series as CPI. The PPI estimates are therefore not a structural
estimate matched through the expectation term, but a semi-structural external-validity
check that changes only the observed inflation index. A measurement mismatch with the
expectation series also remains for core CPI.

\paragraph{Activity gaps (five).} Unemployment gap, BN output gap, HP output gap
($100\times$ log real output HP-filtered, in the same $100$-log-point units as BN),
HP labor-share gap, and inverse markup.

\paragraph{Competition proxy.} The competition series is Gustavo's firm-count measure
(\code{N\_Gustavo}, annual), i.e.\ the \emph{total number of U.S.\ listed firms}. The
main results use PCHIP interpolation to a quarterly value observed every quarter; the
additional results observe the annual value only in Q4 and infer the Q1--Q3 quarterly
states inside the state-space model. The latter is a mixed-frequency specification that
does not treat the interpolated value as data and propagates interpolation uncertainty
into the posterior. The theoretical $N$ is the number of firms \emph{competing
strategically in the same market} and is not the same object, so we use
\code{N\_Gustavo} as an \emph{aggregate proxy for the population of active/listed firms
intended to approximate the theoretical number of competitors}. The two can diverge:
private firms may rise while listed firms fall, industry composition may shift,
merger/delisting rules may change, or foreign and import competition may intensify;
and the economy-wide firm count is not the same as within-industry concentration. We
make this measurement scope explicit and do not equate the total number of listed
firms with a general notion of ``competition'' or with within-industry concentration.
Over the sample the transformed latent trend $\bar N_t$ falls from about $+3.13$ to
$-2.56$ (Figure~\ref{fig:data}(c)), which is why, under $\delta>0$, $\kt$
\emph{declines}.

\paragraph{Unit convention.} The default transform is
$(100\log N-\overline{100\log N})/10$, so one unit of $\bar N$ or $\hat N$ is a
ten-log-point change around the sample mean. The reported
$\delta,\theta,\theta_0,\gamma$ are all on this ten-log-point scale.

\section{Econometric model and estimation}
\label{sec:model}

\subsection{Model variants}
The five models differ only in the restriction on the slope (Table~\ref{tab:models}).

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Model variants.}
\label{tab:models}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
Model & $\kt$ & $\theta_t$ & Role \\
\midrule
\code{ces}             & constant & $0$ & Textbook NKPC benchmark \\
\code{hsa\_steady}     & $\kappa_0+\delta\bar N_t$ & $0$ & \textbf{Main}: trend channel only \\
\code{hsa\_dynamic}    & constant & constant & $\hat N$ channel only \\
\code{hsa\_const\_theta} & $\kappa_0+\delta\bar N_t$ & constant & \code{hsa\_full} with $\gamma=0$ \\
\code{hsa\_full}       & $\kappa_0+\delta\bar N_t$ & $\theta_0+\gamma\bar N_t$ & Full model \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\noindent The main \code{hsa\_steady} uses only the trend channel ($\theta_t=0$). It
is where $\delta$ reads most cleanly, at the cost of dropping the theory's cyclical
entry term. We include \code{hsa\_const\_theta} because the regressor for $\gamma$,
$\hat N\!\cdot\!\bar N$, is nearly collinear (about $98\%$) with the regressor for
$\theta_0$, $\hat N$, so $\gamma$ is not identified.

\subsection{The inflation equation actually estimated}
To put the theoretical equation \eqref{eq:est} directly in regression form, we move
expected inflation to the left-hand side and define
\begin{equation}
y_t\equiv\pi_t-E_t\pi_{t+1},\qquad
a_t\equiv\pi_{t-1}-E_t\pi_{t+1}
\label{eq:ya-def}
\end{equation}
Making the unforecastable component of the activity variable explicit, the estimating
system is
\begin{align}
y_t
 &=\alpha a_t+(\kappa_0+\delta\bar N_t)x_t
   -(\theta_0+\gamma\bar N_t)\hat N_t
   +\lambda_{e\zeta}\zeta_t+\eta_t, \label{eq:estimated-inflation}\\
x_t&=\phi_1x_{t-1}+\zeta_t,\qquad
\eta_t\perp\zeta_t. \label{eq:activity-ar1}
\end{align}
That is, the original NKPC shock decomposes as $e_t=\lambda_{e\zeta}\zeta_t+\eta_t$.
Estimating $\lambda_{e\zeta}$ allows a correlation between the contemporaneous activity
shock and the inflation shock, rather than forcing a simple regression that treats
$x_t$ as exogenous. The saved correlation coefficient is
\begin{equation}
\rho_{e\zeta}
=\frac{\lambda_{e\zeta}\sigma_\zeta}
{\sqrt{\lambda_{e\zeta}^2\sigma_\zeta^2+\sigma_\eta^2}}
\end{equation}
The main \code{hsa\_steady} sets $\theta_0=\gamma=0$; \code{hsa\_dynamic} sets
$\delta=\gamma=0$.

For numerical stability the implementation updates internal coefficients on the
rescaled regressors $x_t/100$ and $x_t\bar N_t/100$ for $\kappa_0$ and $\delta$; the
coefficients are rescaled back by $100$ on saving, so the $\kappa_0,\delta,\kt$ in the
text, tables, and figures are all in the physical units of
\eqref{eq:estimated-inflation}. They must not be multiplied by $100$ or divided by
$100$ again.

\subsection{State-space representation splitting the firm count into trend and cycle}
The observation and transition equations for the firm count are
\begin{align}
N_t^{\mathrm{obs}}&=\bar N_t+\hat N_t+\nu_t,
&\nu_t&\sim N(0,\sigma_N^2), \label{eq:N-measurement}\\
\hat N_t&=\rho_1\hat N_{t-1}+\rho_2\hat N_{t-2}+u_t,
&u_t&\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2), \label{eq:N-gap}\\
\bar N_t&=n+\bar N_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
&\varepsilon_t&\sim N(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2) \label{eq:N-trend}
\end{align}
where $\bar N_t$ is the low-frequency trend with drift $n$ and $\hat N_t$ is a
stationary AR(2) cycle. Rather than a two-step procedure that first filters the
observed firm count into components and then substitutes them into the NKPC, we extract
both states using the firm-count equation and the inflation equation within the same
Gibbs iteration.

\paragraph{Two observation frequencies.} The PCHIP version uses
\eqref{eq:N-measurement} at all 124 quarters. The annual-Q4 version places the annual
firm count in each year's Q4,
\begin{equation}
N_t^{\mathrm{obs}}=
\begin{cases}
(100\log N_{y(t)}^{\mathrm{annual}}-\bar c)/10,&t\in\mathcal T_N\;(\mathrm{Q4}),\\
\mathrm{missing},&t\notin\mathcal T_N\;(\mathrm{Q1--Q3}),
\end{cases}
\qquad |\mathcal T_N|=31,
\label{eq:annual-q4-observation}
\end{equation}
where $\bar c$ is the same centering constant as the PCHIP reference series, keeping
the coefficient units comparable. In Q4 the Kalman update uses two observation
rows---the firm-count equation and the inflation equation---and in Q1--Q3 only the one
inflation row. Because the state transition and prediction continue at every quarter,
the Q1--Q3 $\bar N_t,\hat N_t$ are not simple interpolations but FFBS draws conditioned
on the annual anchors, the state transition, and the inflation equation, updated every
iteration. The inverse-gamma update of $\sigma_N^2$ likewise uses only the 31 finite
Q4 residuals.

For the main \code{hsa\_steady} the state is
\begin{equation}
s_t=(\hat N_t,\hat N_{t-1},\bar N_t)',\qquad
s_t=c+Fs_{t-1}+w_t
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
c=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\n\end{bmatrix},\quad
F=\begin{bmatrix}\rho_1&\rho_2&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
Q=\operatorname{Var}(w_t)
=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_u^2&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&\sigma_\varepsilon^2\end{bmatrix}.
\label{eq:state-matrices}
\end{equation}
Stacking the firm-count observation with the inflation equation net of its known part,
\begin{equation}
y_t^\pi=y_t-\alpha a_t-\kappa_0x_t
-\lambda_{e\zeta}\zeta_t
\end{equation}
gives
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}N_t^{\mathrm{obs}}\\y_t^\pi\end{bmatrix}}_{z_t}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&0&\delta x_t\end{bmatrix}}_{H_t}s_t
+v_t,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(v_t)=
\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_N^2&0\\0&\sigma_\eta^2\end{bmatrix}.
\label{eq:steady-measurement-matrix}
\end{equation}
Conditional on the coefficients and variances this is a linear-Gaussian state-space
model, so $s_{0:T}$ can be drawn jointly by an exact Kalman filter /
forward-filtering backward-sampling (FFBS).

The initial state starts from the fixed prior
\begin{equation}
s_0=(\hat N_0,\hat N_{-1},\bar N_0)'\sim N(m_0,P_0),\qquad
m_0=(0,0,0)',\quad P_0=10I_3
\label{eq:initial-state}
\end{equation}
We do not substitute $N_0^{\mathrm{obs}}$ into $m_0$; the period-0 firm count and
inflation enter the ordinary Kalman observation update. The first AR(2) transition also
actually uses the prior-updated $\hat N_{-1}$. This avoids double-using the initial
observation or dropping the first AR(2) likelihood.

\subsection{Conditional posteriors of the coefficients and variances}
Take the main model as an example, with $\beta=(\alpha,\kappa_0,\delta)'$,
$X_t=(a_t,x_t,x_t\bar N_t)$, and $y_t^*=y_t-\lambda_{e\zeta}\zeta_t$. Under the
independent normal prior $\beta\sim N(b_0,V_0)$, we update jointly from
\begin{align}
V_1&=\left(V_0^{-1}+\frac{X'X}{\sigma_\eta^2}\right)^{-1},\\
b_1&=V_1\left(V_0^{-1}b_0+\frac{X'y^*}{\sigma_\eta^2}\right),\\
\beta\mid\text{rest}&\sim N(b_1,V_1) \label{eq:beta-posterior}
\end{align}
The implementation uses the $100$-rescaled $X$ and coefficients noted above, but the
formula is identical. The baseline estimation imposes no sign restriction, so both
$\delta$ and the end-of-sample $\kt$ can be negative.

We update $\lambda_{e\zeta}$ from the normal conditional posterior of the regression of
$e_t$ on $\zeta_t$. We update $\phi_1$ using not only \eqref{eq:activity-ar1} but also
the information in $e_t=\lambda_{e\zeta}(x_t-\phi_1x_{t-1})+\eta_t$. We draw
$\rho_1,\rho_2$ from a normal conditional posterior truncated to the AR(2) stationary
region,
\begin{equation}
|\rho_2|<1,\qquad \rho_1+\rho_2<1,\qquad \rho_2-\rho_1<1
\end{equation}
The fallback count and rejection rate when no proposal is accepted within 2{,}000 draws
are saved to each run's metadata.

The variance priors are $\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{IG}(a,b)$ (density kernel
$(\sigma^2)^{-(a+1)}\exp(-b/\sigma^2)$), updated from the inverse-gamma conditional
posterior that adds the residual sum of squares. The concrete baseline priors are in
Table~\ref{tab:baseline-priors}.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Baseline priors for the main HSA steady model. Normal distributions show mean
and standard deviation; inverse-gamma distributions show $(a,b)$. The coefficient
priors are common to the other models.}
\label{tab:baseline-priors}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
Block & Parameter & Prior & Interpretation \\
\midrule

Activity eq. & $\phi_1$ & $N(0.7,0.2^2)$ & AR(1) of the activity variable \\

Firm-count state & $(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ & $N(0.5,0.2^2)\times N(-0.5,0.2^2)$ & Truncated to stationary region \\

\midrule
Variances & $\sigma_\eta^2,\sigma_\zeta^2$ & $\operatorname{IG}(2,2),\operatorname{IG}(.001,.001)$ & Inflation / activity shock \\

\noindent For \code{hsa\_dynamic} the shock covariance takes
$\Sigma\sim\operatorname{IW}(8,S_0)$ with $S_0=\operatorname{diag}(3,3,0.06,0.03)$.
Under the default \code{e\_zeta\_only}, the corresponding marginals of this prior apply
to the $(e,\zeta)$ block and the two state variances.

\subsection{What the Kalman filter and FFBS do}
Write the predicted mean and variance at time $t$ as $a_t^s,P_{t|t-1}$ and the filtered
mean and variance as $m_t,P_t$. The forward update for
\eqref{eq:state-matrices}--\eqref{eq:steady-measurement-matrix} is
\begin{align}
a_t^s&=c+Fm_{t-1},&P_{t|t-1}&=FP_{t-1}F'+Q,\\
q_t&=z_t-H_ta_t^s,&S_t&=H_tP_{t|t-1}H_t'+R,\\
K_t&=P_{t|t-1}H_t'S_t^{-1},&m_t&=a_t^s+K_tq_t
\end{align}
The covariance update uses the numerically stable Joseph form. After drawing the
endpoint $s_T\sim N(m_T,P_T)$, we draw the smoothed state path jointly with
\begin{align}
J_t&=P_tF'P_{t+1|t}^{-1},\\
s_t\mid s_{t+1},z_{1:T}
&\sim N\!\left(m_t+J_t(s_{t+1}-c-Fm_t),
P_t-J_tP_{t+1|t}J_t'\right)
\end{align}
for $t=T-1,\ldots,0$. Thus the plotted $\bar N_t,\hat N_t,\kt$ carry the posterior
uncertainty not only of the coefficients but also of the state decomposition.

\subsection{One Gibbs iteration and the differences across models}
One iteration of \code{hsa\_steady} is, in order:
\begin{enumerate}
\item update $(\alpha,\kappa_0,\delta)$ from the current $\bar N_t$ via
\eqref{eq:beta-posterior};
\item update $\lambda_{e\zeta}$ and $\phi_1$, and recompute $\zeta_t,\eta_t$;
\item update $\sigma_\zeta^2,\sigma_\eta^2$;
\item update $(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ and $\sigma_u^2$;
\item update $n$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$, then $\sigma_N^2$;
\item update the entire $s_{0:T}$ by FFBS using the updated coefficients and variances.
\end{enumerate}
CES is a conjugate regression benchmark with no latent firm-count state.\par
\code{hsa\_dynamic} handles the covariance of $r_t=(e_t,\zeta_t,u_t,\varepsilon_t)'$;
under the default \code{e\_zeta\_only} it updates the $2\times2$ block of
$(e_t,\zeta_t)$ and $\sigma_u^2,\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ directly on the constrained
parameter space, rather than zeroing the off-diagonal of an unconstrained
inverse-Wishart draw after the fact.

\code{hsa\_full} contains the state-by-state product $-\gamma\bar N_t\hat N_t$, so it is
not jointly linear-Gaussian in $(\bar N_t,\hat N_t)$ at once. Each iteration therefore
updates $\hat N_{0:T}\mid\bar N_{0:T},\text{rest}$ by AR(2) FFBS and
$\bar N_{0:T}\mid\hat N_{0:T},\text{rest}$ by random-walk FFBS in turn.
\code{hsa\_const\_theta} is the same implementation with $\gamma=0$ fixed. Beyond the
bilinear term of the full model, the burden in both models of identifying the weak
signal of the cyclical state $\hat N_t$ as a separate coefficient is one reason
convergence is weaker for full/const-theta.

\subsection{Iterations, saved draws, and convergence criteria}
Each cell uses two independent chains, with a \emph{total} of 12{,}000 iterations per
chain. We discard the first 4{,}000 as burn-in and save every 5th of the remaining
8{,}000, giving 1{,}600 draws per chain and 3{,}200 draws per cell for diagnostics and
summaries. The main analysis is 75 cells: the baseline 45 (3 price indices $\times$ 3
activity measures $\times$ 5 models) plus the 30 weak/tight-prior cells. Separately, we
estimate 2 inverse-markup CES/HSA-dynamic cells with the same settings.

The acceptance criteria are maximum $\hat R\leq1.01$ and minimum bulk ESS $\geq400$.
HSA steady and CES pass for all reported cells. Many const-theta/full cells and some
dynamic cells fail; they are marked $\dagger$ in the coefficient tables and dropped from
the main inference. The $95\%$ credible intervals are the $2.5\%$ and $97.5\%$
quantiles of the saved draws; the plotted points are posterior means.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering

\section{Main results}
\label{sec:main}

\subsection{The unemployment-gap slope flattens as the firm count falls}
For the baseline \code{hsa\_steady} on the main sample, the core-CPI unemployment
specification gives
\[
\delta=\CoreUnempDelta,
\]
and the Savage--Dickey Bayes factor against $\delta=0$ is
$\mathrm{BF}_{10}=\CoreUnempDeltaBF$. Because $\bar N_t$ falls over the sample, the
implied slope $\kt$ declines monotonically from $\CoreUnempKappaStart$ to
$\CoreUnempKappaEnd$: as the firm count falls (concentration rises), the Phillips curve
flattens, the sign the HSA mechanism predicts. Headline CPI also gives
$\delta=\HeadlineUnempDelta$ ($\mathrm{BF}_{10}=\HeadlineUnempDeltaBF$), so the CPI
result for the unemployment gap is robust to the inflation index. Figure~\ref{fig:kt_unemp}
plots the implied $\kt$ path; its end-of-sample band includes zero, so the accurate
statement is a flattening to near zero rather than a strictly positive residual slope.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{cpi_ppi_report/kappa_t_unemployment_by_inflation.png}
\caption{Time-varying slope $\kt$ for the unemployment gap (posterior mean and $95\%$
band). Under CPI it declines to near zero by the end of the sample, whereas the PPI
band is wide.}
\label{fig:kt_unemp}
\end{figure}

\clearpage
\subsection{Economic magnitude: how many inflation points does the flattening imply?}
\label{sec:magnitude}
We translate the statistical identification of the coefficient into economic units. In
the core-CPI unemployment specification the difference between the start and end slope
is about 0.126. For a change in the unemployment gap of $g$ points, the difference in
the inflation response between the two dates is
$g(\kappa_{\mathrm{start}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{end}})$ points.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Economic magnitude of the time-varying slope (core CPI, unemployment gap).
Each row is the difference between the inflation response around 1982 and around 2012
for the same change in the unemployment gap.}
\label{tab:magnitude}
\input{results/tables/report_additions_en/economic_magnitude.tex}
\end{table}

\noindent For example, a four-point downturn ($x_t=-4$) lowers core inflation by about
0.48 point at the start-of-sample slope, but the response is essentially zero at the
end-of-sample slope. For the actual unemployment-gap series, the difference between the
contribution with the slope fixed at its start value and the contribution with the
time-varying slope is $0.176\;[0.076,0.278]$ point in RMS and
$0.616\;[0.262,0.968]$ point in maximum absolute value. This is a within-model
counterfactual, not a decomposition claiming that the firm-count decline causally
produced the difference.

\subsection{Slope level: is the curve alive?}
The slope at average competition $\kappa_0$ for the unemployment gap has a credible
interval that excludes zero for headline and core CPI; for PPI the interval is wide.
Because $\delta$ is the \emph{time variation} of the slope and $\kappa_0$ is the
\emph{level} at the centered average firm count, the two must be distinguished. The
slope level and competition dependence for the output-gap specifications are collected
in Appendix~\ref{app:output-gaps}.

\section{Direct test on PPI}
\label{sec:ppi-direct}

\subsection{Why look at PPI?}
The Fujiwara--Matsuyama equation is derived for producer-price inflation. Even if we
obtain a positive $\delta$ for CPI, it is not a general upstream HSA effect if it is
specific to retail/distribution margins, pass-through to consumer prices, or the price
composition. We therefore hold the sample, activity measure, firm-count series, and
expectation series fixed and change only the observed inflation index to PPI.

\subsection{Results}
The HSA-steady unemployment specification gives $\delta=\PPIUnempDelta$,
$\mathrm{BF}_{10}=\PPIUnempDeltaBF$. The point estimate is positive but the $95\%$
credible interval includes zero. The HP and BN point estimates are small and negative,
and again the intervals include zero. The Bayes factors for all three specifications
are near one. We therefore read this, more strongly than ``the direction is partly
consistent but the precision is insufficient,'' as: there is at present no PPI evidence
supporting $\delta\neq0$.

PPI is more affected than CPI by energy, imported raw materials, and industry
composition, and its posterior intervals are wide. This is not a reason to discard the
non-result. Rather, that the low-frequency relationship obtained for CPI does not
appear clearly in upstream prices is the substantive finding from adding PPI.

\subsection{Limits from expected inflation}
Because the SPF has no PPI expectation, the PPI specifications use the common external
expectation series. The design is transparent as a comparison that changes only the
left-hand side, but it does not match the theoretical equation through expectation
formation. If a PPI forecast (e.g.\ from the Livingston Survey) could be connected, an
auxiliary estimate matched through the expectation term would be possible. We do not
call the current results ``a full estimate of the PPI structural equation.''

\section{The CES slope bias and the constant-slope benchmark}
\label{sec:ces-hsa-bias}\label{sec:bench}

\subsection{Theoretical prediction and its empirical counterpart}
Fujiwara--Matsuyama (2026) show that because endogenous entry generates a cost-push
term through strategic complementarity, a CES-type equation that regresses inflation on
real marginal cost alone under-estimates the NKPC slope. In our HSA-dynamic
representation, moving expected inflation to the left-hand side gives
\begin{equation}
y_t=\alpha a_t+\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}x_t+q_t+e_t,
\qquad q_t=-\theta\hat N_t,
\label{eq:bias-hsa}
\end{equation}
where $y_t=\pi_t-\mathbb E_t\pi_{t+1}$ and $a_t=\pi_{t-1}-\mathbb E_t\pi_{t+1}$. When
the CES equation omits $q_t$,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}})
=\operatorname{plim}(\hat\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\hat\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}})
=\frac{\tilde x'\tilde q}{\tilde x'\tilde x},
\label{eq:bias-ovb}
\end{equation}
where tildes denote residuals after removing $a_t$ and the activity shock
$\zeta_t=x_t-\phi_1x_{t-1}$. The theory predicts \eqref{eq:bias-ovb} is negative, i.e.\
$\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}<0$.

To keep this correspondence sharp, separately from the slack measures of the main
results we use the BN-decomposed inverse markup as a proxy for real marginal cost and
re-estimate CES and HSA dynamic with the same sample, priors, and MCMC settings. For
each HSA posterior draw we form $q_t^{(s)}=-\theta^{(s)}\hat N_t^{(s)}$ and directly
compute the bias in \eqref{eq:bias-ovb}. Because the CES--HSA difference is a comparison
across separately estimated posteriors, we build a Monte Carlo distribution of the
difference by randomly permuting the HSA draws with a fixed seed.

\subsection{Estimation results}
For the inverse-markup specification that corresponds directly to the theory,
\begin{align*}
\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}&=\BiasDirectCES,&
\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\BiasDirectHSA,\\
\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\BiasDirectDifference,&
\Pr(\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}<0)&=\BiasDirectProbability,\\
B_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\BiasDirectOVB,&
\Pr(B_{\mathrm{HSA}}<0)&=\BiasDirectOVBProbability
\end{align*}
The CES--HSA difference does not show a negative bias. The omitted-variable bias
implied by HSA itself also has a point estimate of the sign opposite to the theory
(positive), with a credible interval that includes zero.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{CES--HSA-dynamic slope comparison and the omitted-variable bias implied by
HSA. Each interval is a $95\%$ credible interval. $\dagger$ marks that at least one of
CES or HSA dynamic is outside the convergence criteria.}
\label{tab:ces-hsa-bias}
\tiny
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{results/tables/cpi_ppi_report_en/ces_hsa_kappa_bias.tex}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Verdict.} The inverse-markup row passes the convergence criteria for both
models, but the slope intervals are wide and neither the CES--HSA difference nor the
within-model OVB supports the negative sign the theory predicts. The three auxiliary
rows using the unemployment gap give the same conclusion. This does not amount to a
refutation of the theory: the inverse markup is an aggregate series rather than
firm-level real marginal cost, and HSA dynamic is not a joint estimate of the full
theoretical model. What we can say from this paper is only that \emph{in the current
data and semi-structural model, we do not obtain an estimate corresponding to the
theory paper's prediction of a negative bias in the CES slope}.

\subsection{Constant-slope benchmark (\code{ces})}
As a benchmark for the time-varying result of Section~\ref{sec:main}, we also estimate
the constant-slope models. The full model-by-model coefficient tables for the
unemployment gap, and the corresponding prior-sensitivity table, are collected in
Appendix~\ref{app:model-tables}.
\paragraph{CES (constant $\kappa$).} CES is the constant-slope benchmark. Among the
converged cells, the core-CPI $\kappa$ interval sits on the positive side, while
headline CPI and PPI include zero. CES measures the existence of the average curve but
does not explain the flattening. The prior-vs-posterior of the slope
(Figure~\ref{fig:kappa_pp}) shows CES's constant $\kappa$ and \code{hsa\_steady}'s
slope at average competition $\kappa_0$, both sharply updated by the data and sitting
just above zero.

CES's constant slope $\kappa$ and \code{hsa\_steady}'s slope at average competition

\section{Does the time-varying slope improve fit over the constant slope?}
\label{sec:mc}
We compare CES (constant $\kappa$) against \code{hsa\_steady} (slope varying with the
firm count) by two criteria: an in-sample fit score and the Savage--Dickey Bayes factor
for $\delta\neq 0$ (Table~\ref{tab:mc}).

\paragraph{In-sample plug-in fit score.} We evaluate the inflation equation at
posterior-mean parameters and states (bars denote posterior means),
\begin{equation}
\hat\pi_t=\bar\alpha\,\pi_{t-1}+(1-\bar\alpha)\,\mathbb{E}_t\pi_{t+1}+\bar\kt\,x_t,
\qquad \bar\kt=\bar\kappa_0+\bar\delta\,\bar N_t
\;\;(\text{CES: }\bar\kt=\bar\kappa),
\end{equation}
and score the fit by the Gaussian log-likelihood of the residuals
$r_t=\pi_t-\hat\pi_t$ with $\bar\sigma_e^2$ the posterior-mean shock variance:
\begin{equation}
S=-\frac{T}{2}\log\!\big(2\pi\bar\sigma_e^2\big)-\frac{1}{2\bar\sigma_e^2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_t^2 .
\end{equation}
This is an \emph{in-sample plug-in} score: it reuses the estimation sample and the
posterior means, and is neither an out-of-sample forecast nor a posterior predictive
density. It is used only as a rough comparative fit diagnostic; a proper predictive
comparison (LOO, WAIC, rolling one-step forecasts, or an integrated log predictive
density) is left for future work. In the unemployment specification the time-varying
slope improves this score over CES.

\paragraph{Bayes factor (Savage--Dickey), stated precisely.} We test $\delta=0$
\emph{within the HSA state model}: $M_1$ is \code{hsa\_steady} with $\delta$ free and
$M_0$ is the same model with $\delta=0$. The Savage--Dickey identity gives
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{BF}_{10}=\frac{p(\delta=0)}{\pi(\delta=0\mid y)},\qquad
p(\delta=0)=\frac{1}{\sigma_\delta\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac{1}{0.02\sqrt{2\pi}}\approx 19.95
\;\;(\delta\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\delta^2)),
\end{equation}
with the posterior ordinate estimated by a Gaussian kernel density on the draws
$\{\delta^{(s)}\}$, $\hat\pi(\delta=0\mid y)=\tfrac{1}{Sh}\sum_s\phi\!\big((0-\delta^{(s)})/h\big)$.
Three cautions. (i) This is \emph{not} a CES-vs-HSA marginal-likelihood ratio: CES and
HSA also differ in the latent-$N$ block, which the SDDR holds fixed, so we keep the
comparison inside the HSA state model. (ii) The theory is one-sided ($\delta>0$); the
two-sided $\mathrm{BF}_{10}$ is conservative. (iii) The zero-point posterior density is
a KDE estimate; the ordering across specifications is insensitive to the bandwidth, but
the exact magnitudes are not, so we report them to a few significant figures.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Constant vs.\ time-varying slope: is $\delta\neq0$? Posterior mean of $\delta$
$[95\%$ CI$]$ with the Savage--Dickey Bayes factor $\mathrm{BF}_{10}$ for $\delta\neq0$
within the HSA state model in parentheses (\code{hsa\_steady}, baseline priors,
quarterly, unrestricted). Values are auto-generated from the current posteriors;
$\mathrm{BF}_{10}>1$ favors a concentration-dependent slope.}
\label{tab:mc}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Activity measure & Headline CPI & Core CPI & PPI \\
\midrule
Unemployment gap & \HeadlineUnempDelta\ (\HeadlineUnempDeltaBF) & \CoreUnempDelta\ (\CoreUnempDeltaBF) & \PPIUnempDelta\ (\PPIUnempDeltaBF) \\
Output gap (HP)  & \HeadlineHPDelta\ (\HeadlineHPDeltaBF) & \CoreHPDelta\ (\CoreHPDeltaBF) & \PPIHPDelta\ (\PPIHPDeltaBF) \\
Output gap (BN)  & \HeadlineBNDelta\ (\HeadlineBNDeltaBF) & \CoreBNDelta\ (\CoreBNDeltaBF) & \PPIBNDelta\ (\PPIBNDeltaBF) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Verdict.} For the unemployment gap, allowing the slope to vary with the firm
count improves the in-sample fit score and the Bayes factor favors $\delta\neq0$
strongly under both CPI indices. For the headline output gaps the gain is marginal,
consistent with the appendix tables: a positive competition dependence appears only in
the core-CPI HP specification, not in BN. For the labor-share gap and inverse markup
there is no inflation signal, so constant and time-varying slopes fit equally well. We
stress that this is an in-sample fit comparison, not evidence of out-of-sample
predictive gains.

\paragraph{Limits of the model comparison.} We read the Savage--Dickey ratios only as
the point null $\delta=0$ \emph{within the HSA state model}; they are not a CES-vs-HSA
marginal-likelihood ratio. The in-sample LPPD and RMSE conditioned on the latent states
are likewise not out-of-sample predictions, so they are not used as grounds to select a
more complex model. The automatic Chib marginal likelihood is contaminated for
annual-Q4 blocks by a missing-N bug (Section~\ref{sec:status}) and is excluded from
this table.

\section{Estimating quarterly firm counts from Q4-only observations}
\label{sec:annual-q4-results}
Against the results so far, which use the PCHIP-interpolated value as data every
quarter, this section applies the mixed-frequency observation scheme of
\eqref{eq:annual-q4-observation} and reports the results in the same order. The 3 price
indices, 3 activity measures, 5 models, 3 priors, and the inverse-markup slope-bias
diagnostic are unchanged. We newly estimate the 61 HSA cells with 12{,}000 iterations
and 2 chains. Because CES contains neither $N_t$ nor a latent firm-count state, its
likelihood and posterior do not change with the observation frequency, so we reuse it as
a shared reference across the 16 CES cells. In the CES--HSA comparisons below, the CES
column is therefore the same benchmark and only the HSA column is annual-Q4 estimated.

\subsection{What the annual-Q4 estimation does}
\label{sec:annual-q4-method}
The annual-Q4 variant is a \emph{mixed-frequency state-space estimation}, not an
interpolate-then-regress procedure. The distinction is the whole point: the PCHIP
version inserts a smooth deterministic curve and treats it as if the firm count were
observed every quarter, which injects manufactured within-year variation and
understates uncertainty; the annual-Q4 version instead treats the sub-annual firm
count as \emph{latent} and lets the model infer it.

Concretely, the firm count enters the observation equation only in the 31 fourth
quarters, and Q1--Q3 are coded as missing (\eqref{eq:annual-q4-observation}). The
Kalman filter handles this exactly by varying the observation block by quarter. In a
Q4 the update uses both rows of \eqref{eq:steady-measurement-matrix}---the firm-count
row and the inflation row---so the annual anchor pins the level of $\bar N_t$. In
Q1--Q3 the firm-count row is dropped and only the inflation row remains, i.e.\ the
measurement update for that quarter carries just the information that the slope
$\delta x_t$ places on $\bar N_t$; the state prediction and transition
\eqref{eq:state-matrices} nonetheless run at every quarter, propagating the latent
$(\hat N_t,\hat N_{t-1},\bar N_t)$ forward between the annual observations. Each Gibbs
iteration then draws the \emph{entire} quarterly path $s_{0:T}$ by FFBS, conditioned on
the 31 annual anchors, the quarterly inflation and activity data, the state dynamics,
and the current coefficients and variances. The Q1--Q3 firm counts are therefore
posterior draws, not deterministic interpolations, and their uncertainty flows through
to the posterior of $\delta$ and the $\kt$ path.

\paragraph{The mixed-frequency Kalman step, in equations.} Yes, the state block is an
exact Kalman filter---the same one as in Section~\ref{sec:model}; annual-Q4 changes only
the observation row that is available each quarter. Let $\mathcal T_N$ be the 31 Q4
quarters and, as before, write the inflation observation net of its known part as
$y_t^\pi=y_t-\alpha a_t-\kappa_0 x_t-\lambda_{e\zeta}\zeta_t$. The observation triple
$(z_t,H_t,R_t)$ switches with the calendar quarter:
\begin{equation}
(z_t,H_t,R_t)=
\begin{cases}
\left(\begin{bmatrix}N_t^{\mathrm{obs}}\\[1pt] y_t^\pi\end{bmatrix},\;
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\ 0&0&\delta x_t\end{bmatrix},\;
\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_N^2&0\\ 0&\sigma_\eta^2\end{bmatrix}\right),
& t\in\mathcal T_N\ (\mathrm{Q4}),\\[2.4ex]
\left(\,y_t^\pi,\;\;
\begin{bmatrix}0&0&\delta x_t\end{bmatrix},\;\;\sigma_\eta^2\right),
& t\notin\mathcal T_N\ (\mathrm{Q1\text{--}Q3}).
\end{cases}
\label{eq:annual-q4-obsblock}
\end{equation}
The same linear-Gaussian recursion then runs at \emph{every} quarter, with only the row
dimension of the update changing (two rows in Q4, one in Q1--Q3):
\begin{align*}
m_{t\mid t-1}&=c+Fm_{t-1}, & P_{t\mid t-1}&=FP_{t-1}F'+Q,\\
v_t&=z_t-H_tm_{t\mid t-1}, & S_t&=H_tP_{t\mid t-1}H_t'+R_t,\\
K_t&=P_{t\mid t-1}H_t'S_t^{-1}, & m_t&=m_{t\mid t-1}+K_tv_t,\\
P_t&=(I-K_tH_t)P_{t\mid t-1}\ \ (\text{Joseph form}). & &
\end{align*}
In Q1--Q3 the prediction still advances $\bar N_t,\hat N_t$ through
\eqref{eq:state-matrices}, but the firm-count row is simply absent and the only
measurement information is the scalar $y_t^\pi$ loading on $\bar N_t$ through $\delta
x_t$. The smoothed path $s_{0:T}$ is drawn by the same forward-filtering
backward-sampling pass as the PCHIP version. Finally, the measurement-variance update
uses only the finite Q4 residuals,
\begin{equation}
r_t^N=N_t^{\mathrm{obs}}-\hat N_t-\bar N_t\ \ (t\in\mathcal T_N),\qquad
\sigma_N^2\mid\cdot\sim\operatorname{IG}\!\Big(a_N+\tfrac{|\mathcal T_N|}{2},\;
b_N+\tfrac12\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_N}(r_t^N)^2\Big),\qquad |\mathcal T_N|=31.
\label{eq:annual-q4-sigmaN}
\end{equation}
Setting $\mathcal T_N=\{1,\dots,T\}$ (every quarter observed) recovers the PCHIP filter
exactly; annual-Q4 is that filter with 93 of the 124 firm-count rows removed.

In short, within the same Gibbs sweep the annual-Q4 estimation jointly updates:
\begin{itemize}
\item the coefficients $(\alpha,\kappa_0,\delta,\dots)$ from \eqref{eq:beta-posterior},
exactly as in the PCHIP version;
\item the shock and measurement variances, with $\sigma_N^2$ updated from only the 31
finite Q4 residuals;
\item the full latent path $\bar N_{0:T},\hat N_{0:T}$ (all 124 quarters, including the
93 unobserved ones) by FFBS.
\end{itemize}
CES carries no latent firm-count state and no $N_t$ term, so its likelihood and
posterior are unchanged by the observation frequency; it is reused as the common
reference. The practical cost is that not pretending the quarterly count is observed
widens the intervals and lowers the effective sample size for the state block---which is
itself the measurement uncertainty that the PCHIP version hides rather than a defect of
the estimator.

\subsection{CES--HSA slope bias}
For the inverse-markup specification that corresponds directly to the theory,
\begin{align*}
\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}&=\AnnualBiasDirectCES,&
\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\AnnualBiasDirectHSA,\\
\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\AnnualBiasDirectDifference,&
\Pr(\kappa_{\mathrm{CES}}-\kappa_{\mathrm{HSA}}<0)&=\AnnualBiasDirectProbability,\\
B_{\mathrm{HSA}}&=\AnnualBiasDirectOVB,&
\Pr(B_{\mathrm{HSA}}<0)&=\AnnualBiasDirectOVBProbability.
\end{align*}
The CES coefficient is identical to the PCHIP version, while the HSA coefficient and the
$\hat N_t$ of \eqref{eq:bias-ovb} are computed from the annual-Q4 posterior. This keeps
the smooth quarterly variation produced by interpolation out of the omitted-variable
bias diagnostic. Because the annual-Q4 HSA dynamic, including the inverse markup, is
outside the whole-run convergence criteria, the difference and OVB below are an
additional diagnostic and not a formal test of the theoretical prediction.

For the annual-Q4 version too, the conclusions we adopt are limited to cells meeting the

identifies the quarterly cycle $\hat N_t$ and its coefficient from a firm count observed
only annually carries little information. The widening intervals and lower ESS are
themselves evidence of the measurement uncertainty hidden when PCHIP is taken as given.
Also, because the $\delta$ interval for the CPI unemployment specification includes zero
under the HSA-steady tight prior, the annual-Q4 version is not prior-invariant either.
The same comparison by output gap is in Appendix~\ref{app:annual-output-gaps}.

\section{Scope condition and the limits of identification}
\label{sec:scope}
For honesty we state where the main result does \emph{not} hold and what it can and
cannot claim.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Not identified for PPI.} Switching to PPI, closer to the theory's
left-hand side, makes $\delta$ include zero for all activity measures. Despite the
measurement limitation that no PPI expectation exists, we cannot claim that the CPI
relationship holds generally at the price-setting stage.
\item \textbf{The complex models do not converge.} Many const-theta/full cells are
outside the acceptance criteria, so we cannot claim to have demonstrated the
cyclical-entry channel or $\gamma$.
\item \textbf{The annual-Q4 joint posterior does not converge.} The CPI $\delta$
marginal chains mix well and give a positive point estimate close to the PCHIP version,
but the ESS/Rhat of the AR(2) coefficients and latent-state paths are outside the
criteria. The annual-Q4 result is therefore an important additional diagnostic of
interpolation dependence, but at this stage does not count as a robustness check that
confirms the main result.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Not a causal effect.} $\bar N_t$ is a near-monotone low-frequency trend, so
on this design $\delta$ cannot be separated from other things that trended over the
same decades: the Volcker monetary-policy regime change, the anchoring of inflation
expectations, changes in labor-market institutions and unionization, globalization and
import competition, changes in the frequency of price adjustment, or a simple time
trend / structural break. The most we can say is that \emph{the low-frequency decline
in the firm count and the decline in inflation's sensitivity to the unemployment gap
occurred together, with a sign consistent with the HSA theory}. We therefore avoid
``competition causes flattening'' and ``we identify the mechanism.''

\section{Robustness}
\label{sec:robust}
We judge robustness on three points: (i) how the sign, interval, and magnitude change
under alternative priors, (ii) whether the result survives switching the price index to
PPI, and (iii) whether the same conclusion holds using only converged runs. The prior
check re-estimates \emph{every cell} under baseline, weak, and tight priors
(Table~\ref{tab:current-priors}); it is a genuine re-estimation of the current runs, not
a re-weighting of a single posterior.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Three-prior sensitivity of the current results (unemployment-gap
specification): $\delta$ under baseline, weak, and tight priors, by model and price
index. Each cell is a separate re-estimation of the current runs, not a re-weighting.
$\dagger$ marks cells outside the convergence criteria and not interpreted.}
\label{tab:current-priors}
\tiny
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{results/tables/cpi_ppi_report_en/prior_sensitivity_compact.tex}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{HSA steady.} The headline-CPI and core-CPI $\delta$ keep a positive sign
under baseline/weak/tight, with posterior intervals on the positive side. But the
interval is wide under weak and shrinks toward zero under tight, so it is not fully
prior-invariant. The core-CPI baseline carries the strongest weight of evidence. PPI
includes zero under all three priors and does not provide external confirmation of the
CPI result.

\paragraph{Model variants.} The $\dagger$ cells of const-theta/full are not counted as
robustness evidence even when the sign matches steady. Dynamic is also short of ESS in
some cells. Before claiming ``the result survives'' under added complexity, convergence
must be established through reparameterization or longer independent chains.

\paragraph{Period robustness.} The state equation assumes consecutive quarters. We do
not use the old treatment that deletes an interior span and compresses what precedes and
follows. The current 77 runs are full-sample comparisons; until a separate contiguous
subsample estimation of the corrected revision is done, we do not include pre-2008 or
post-1988 numbers in the conclusions.

\section{Conclusion}
Over 1982--2012 in the United States, the low-frequency decline in the number of listed
firms and the decline in inflation's sensitivity to the unemployment gap moved together.
We read this as theory-consistent time-series evidence, not a causal effect.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Sign consistent with HSA.} For the core-CPI unemployment specification
$\delta=\CoreUnempDelta$ ($\mathrm{BF}_{10}=\CoreUnempDeltaBF$); a falling firm count
implies a flatter slope, as the theory predicts.
\item \textbf{Economically sizable flattening.} The implied $\kt$ falls from
$\CoreUnempKappaStart$ to $\CoreUnempKappaEnd$; the start-to-end response to a one-point
unemployment gap differs by about 0.126 point.
\item \textbf{Core CPI aligns the output gap.} Under core CPI the HP output gap shows the
same positive sign; BN stays inconclusive.
\item \textbf{Not confirmed for PPI.} The unemployment specification gives
$\delta=\PPIUnempDelta$, with the interval including zero for all activity measures, so
the relationship is not a general upstream (price-setting-stage) effect.
\item \textbf{No CES-slope bias found.} The theory's predicted negative bias of the CES
slope is not supported: both the CES--HSA difference and the HSA-implied omitted-variable
bias have intervals including zero, with, if anything, positive point estimates.
\item \textbf{Cyclical-entry channel unconfirmed.} Many \code{const\_theta}/\code{full}
cells do not converge and the converged entry coefficients include zero.
\item \textbf{Annual-Q4 is provisional.} The CPI $\delta$ marginal posterior stays
positive under Q4-only observation, but the latent states and AR(2) block miss the
convergence criteria, so this is a sensitivity diagnostic, not a confirmed robustness
check.
\item \textbf{Identification caveat.} The variation is concentrated in the 1980s and
$\bar N_t$ is nearly collinear with a linear trend, so $\delta$ is an association, not a
causal effect.
\end{itemize}

\section{Status and open items}
\label{sec:status}
\paragraph{Estimation status (auto-generated).}
This draft uses the \ReportRunCount{} runs of revision \ReportEstimationRevision{}.
Of these, \ReportWarningCount{} runs fail the acceptance criteria (maximum
$\hat R\leq1.01$ and minimum bulk ESS $\geq400$) and their coefficients are not used
for the main conclusions. All headline estimates, tables, and figures are generated
automatically from the saved posteriors; no numbers from earlier revisions are read
in. In addition, an annual-Q4 variant---in which the firm count is observed only in
Q4 and the intervening quarterly states are inferred---is assembled from \emph{new}
estimates of the 61 HSA cells and a shared reference of 16 CES cells that do not use
the firm count. Of the \AnnualReportRunCount{} cells in the annual-Q4 comparison,
\AnnualReportWarningCount{} fail the same convergence criteria.

\paragraph{Settled in the current revision.} The positive $\delta$ and flattening $\kt$
for the CPI unemployment specification of HSA steady; the positive sign of the core-CPI
HP specification and the non-result of BN, separated into the appendix; the non-results
of the three PPI activity specifications; the three-prior sensitivity; the convergence
of CES/HSA steady; the economic magnitude; and the CES--HSA slope-bias diagnostic via the
inverse markup. The HSA
results settled here are the PCHIP version. The 61 annual-Q4 HSA cells are estimated in
this setting but retain the convergence issues below.

\paragraph{Open (empirical / econometric).}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Causal identification.} The horse race against a linear time trend cannot
distinguish the two. Before any claim beyond association, add quadratic trends,
structural-break dummies, and placebo interactions.
\item \textbf{Expectation mismatch.} Beyond core-matched expected inflation, connect a
PPI forecast series (e.g.\ the Livingston Survey) so the expectation term matches the
price index.
\item \textbf{Predictive evaluation.} Replace the in-sample plug-in fit score with
LOO/WAIC or rolling out-of-sample forecasts.
\item \textbf{Period robustness.} Re-estimate the current revision using only contiguous
quarters. The pre-2008/post-1988 numbers from earlier revisions are not used for the
conclusions of this paper.
\item \textbf{Bayes-factor robustness.} In addition to the two-sided SDDR, report the
one-sided ($\delta>0$) evaluation and the KDE bandwidth sensitivity.
\item \textbf{Annual-Q4 state block.} The marginal chains of $\delta,\kappa_0$ are good,
but $\rho_1,\rho_2$ and some time points of $\bar N_t,\hat N_t$ have low ESS / high Rhat.
Consider reparameterization, longer independent chains, and priors that relax the weak
identification of the state equation.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Open (computational).}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Automatic marginal likelihood.} The Chib marginal likelihood is excluded
from the automatic tables because the integration over the latent states and the
normalization of the truncated prior are unverified. It is not used for model selection
until a verified implementation exists.
\item \textbf{Weak convergence of const-theta/full.} The cells to watch are dropped from
the main inference. Consider reparameterization, longer independent chains, and
identifying restrictions.
\item \textbf{Weak identification of $\gamma$.} An identification strategy is needed to
relax the collinearity between $\hat N\bar N$ and $\hat N$.
\end{itemize}

results by price index (3) and model (5) for each definition. The slope is the constant
$\kappa$ for CES/HSA dynamic and the slope at average competition $\kappa_0$ for the
other HSA models. $\delta$ is the sensitivity of the slope to the firm-count trend, and

\subsection{HP output gap}
For HSA steady the headline-CPI $\delta$ is near zero, while core CPI is positive:
\begin{equation*}
\delta_{\mathrm{Core,HP}}=\CoreHPDelta,
\qquad \mathrm{BF}_{10}=\CoreHPDeltaBF.
\end{equation*}
The PPI $\delta=\PPIHPDelta$ includes zero. The positive competition dependence of the
HP specification is therefore limited to core CPI and is not a result for price indices
in general.

\subsection{BN output gap}
For HSA steady the $\delta$ point estimates are negative for headline CPI, positive for
core CPI, and negative for PPI, but all three $95\%$ credible intervals include zero
(headline $\HeadlineBNDelta$, core $\CoreBNDelta$, PPI $\PPIBNDelta$). Each
$\mathrm{BF}_{10}$ is also about one, so the BN specification provides no evidence for a
competition dependence of the slope.

\paragraph{How to read the whole.} HP core CPI agrees in direction with the CPI result
for the unemployment gap, but HP headline, HP PPI, and all price indices of BN do not
support it. And because const-theta/full have many cells outside the convergence
criteria, we do not count sign agreement in the complex models as robustness evidence.
The output-gap results are not a claim that ``the result always holds across activity
measures'' but a sensitivity analysis showing which combinations of measurement and
price index the result depends on.
